records.text: Heliodorus immediately began his journey, ostensibly to inspect the cities of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, but actually to carry out the king’s intention.

When he arrived in Jerusalem and was cordially received by the city’s high priest, he related the information that had been given and explained why he was there. He asked whether these things were really so.
The high priest explained that they were deposits belonging to widows and orphans,

and that some also belonged to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, a man of very high standing. Thus the impious Simon had misrepresented matters. In all there were four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold.

It was utterly impossible, he said, that those who had trusted in the holiness of the place and in the dignity and inviolability of the temple honoured throughout the whole world should suffer injustice.
But Heliodorus, because of his royal instructions, insisted that the money must certainly be taken into the royal treasury.
He appointed a day and went in to arrange the inspection of these things. There was no small anguish throughout the city.

The priests threw themselves down before the altar in their priestly robes, calling to heaven upon the One who had legislated about deposits, that He would keep them safe for those who had entrusted them.
Women, girded with sackcloth beneath their breasts, thronged the streets. Of the secluded virgins, some ran together to the gateways, some to the walls, and others leaned out through the windows.
All of them stretched their hands toward heaven and offered their entreaty.
It was pitiful to see the mingled multitude falling prostrate, and the high priest waiting in great anguish.
So they called on the all-powerful Lord to keep the entrusted property safe and fully secure for those who had entrusted it.
In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Arthasastha, the wine was before me. I took the wine and gave it to the king, and there was no other person before him.
The king said to me, “What are you asking for?” I prayed to the God of heaven,
and said to the king, “If it pleases the king, and if your servant finds favor before you, send him to Judah, to the city of my fathers’ tombs, and I will rebuild it.”
With threat Thou wilt diminish the earth, and in fury Thou wilt bring nations down.
Thou didst go out for Thy people’s salvation, to save Thine anointed ones. Thou didst cast death upon the heads of lawless people and didst raise bonds up to the neck. Diapsalma.
Thou didst cut the heads of rulers in bewilderment; they will be shaken in it. They will open their bridles like a poor person eating secretly.
Thou didst drive Thy horses into the sea as they troubled much water.

For the fig tree will not bear fruit, and vines will have no produce; the olive’s labor will fail, and fields will not produce food. Sheep have failed for lack of food, and there are no cattle at feeding troughs.
But I will exult in the Lord; I will rejoice in God my Savior.
The Lord God is my strength; He will set my feet toward completion and lead me onto the heights, to conquer in His song.
“And now,” says the Lord your God, “turn to Me with your whole heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning.”
Tear your hearts, not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, because He is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy, and relents concerning calamities.
Who knows whether He will turn and relent and leave a blessing behind Him, a sacrifice and drink offering for the Lord our God?
Then the Lord became jealous for His land and spared His people.
Heliodorus, however, was carrying out his decision.

When he was already there at the treasury with his bodyguards, the Sovereign of spirits and of all authority made a great manifestation. All who had dared accompany him were struck with awe at God’s power and were overcome by faintness and cowardice.

For there appeared to them a horse with a fearsome rider, adorned with the finest harness. Rushing forcefully forward, it struck at Heliodorus with its forehooves; its rider appeared to wear a full suit of golden armour.

Two other young men appeared to him, remarkable in strength, most beautiful in glory, and splendid in clothing. They stood on either side of him and flogged him without ceasing, raining many blows upon him.
He suddenly fell to the ground, and deep darkness enveloped him. They picked him up and placed him on a litter.
The man who had just entered that treasury with a large retinue and all his bodyguard was carried out, unable to help himself. They plainly recognized God’s sovereignty.
Through the divine action he lay speechless, deprived of every hope and means of deliverance.

But they blessed the Lord, who had wonderfully honoured His own place. The temple that a little earlier had been full of dread and turmoil was filled with joy and gladness when the Almighty Lord appeared.
Some of Heliodorus’s companions quickly begged Onias to call upon the Most High to grant life to the man who lay at his last breath.
The high priest, fearing that the king might form the opinion that the Jews had perpetrated some wrongdoing against Heliodorus, offered a sacrifice for the man’s deliverance.

While the high priest was making propitiation, the same young men again appeared to Heliodorus, clothed in the same garments. They stood and said, “Give many thanks to Onias the high priest, for it is because of him that the Lord has granted you life.
You, having been scourged from heaven, proclaim to everyone God’s majestic might.” Having said this, they became invisible.
He bore witness to everyone about the deeds of the greatest God that he had seen with his own eyes.
The Lord commanded a great sea creature to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the sea creature’s belly three days and three nights.
Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the sea creature’s belly,
and said: “In my affliction I cried to the Lord my God, and He listened to me. From the belly of Hades Thou didst hear the voice of my cry.
Thou didst cast me into the depths of the heart of the sea, and rivers encircled me. All Thy billows and Thy waves passed over me.
I said, ‘I have been thrust away from Thine eyes. Shall I again look toward Thy holy sanctuary?’
Water poured around me up to my life; the uttermost abyss encircled me; my head sank into clefts of mountains.
I descended into a land whose bars are everlasting restraints; and let the ruin of my life rise up, Lord my God.
The sea creature was commanded, and it cast Jonah out onto dry land.
When Seleucus departed this life and Antiochus, called Epiphanes, took over the kingdom, Jason, Onias’s brother, obtained the high priesthood by fraud.
In an audience he promised the king three hundred sixty talents of silver, and eighty talents from another source of revenue.

Beyond these he promised to pay a further one hundred fifty if he were permitted by royal authority to establish a gymnasium and a training institution for young men, and to enroll the people in Jerusalem as Antiochenes.
When the king consented and Jason gained office, he immediately turned his fellow countrymen toward the Greek manner of life.

He set aside the benevolent royal concessions established for the Jews through John, the father of Eupolemus, who had undertaken the embassy to the Romans for friendship and alliance. Abolishing the lawful forms of civic life, he introduced unlawful customs.
For he eagerly established a gymnasium immediately beneath the citadel and brought the most distinguished young men under his direction to wear the broad-brimmed hat.
There was such an upsurge of Hellenism and advance of foreign ways because of the surpassing impurity of the impious Jason, who was no high priest,
They regarded their ancestral honours as nothing and considered Greek distinctions the finest.
For this reason a difficult crisis overtook them: those whose ways they admired and whom they wished to resemble in everything became their enemies and punishers.
For acting impiously against the divine laws is no light matter; the ensuing time will show this.
“And now appease the face of your God and plead with Him. These things have happened in your hands. Will I show favor to any of you?” says the Lord Almighty.
“For even among you doors will be shut, and you will not kindle My altar for nothing. I have no desire for you,” says the Lord Almighty, “and I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands.”

“For from the sun’s rising to its setting, My name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is brought to My name, together with a pure sacrifice, because My name is great among the nations,” says the Lord Almighty.
“But you profane it by your saying, ‘The Lord’s table is polluted, and the foods placed upon it are despised.’

“And you said, ‘These things are from hardship,’ and I blew them away,” says the Lord Almighty. “You were bringing things seized by force, the lame and the afflicted. If you bring the sacrifice, shall I accept these things from your hands?” says the Lord Almighty.

“Cursed is one who was able, and had a male in his flock and a vow concerning it, yet sacrifices a damaged animal to the Lord. For I am a great King,” says the Lord Almighty, “and My name is manifest among the nations.”
The words of Neemias son of Achalia. In the month of Chaseelou, in the twentieth year, I was in Sousan abira,
and Anani, one of my brothers, came, he and men of Judah. I asked them about those who had been saved, who remained from the captivity, and about Jerusalem.

They said to me, “The remaining people who were left from the captivity there in the country are in great distress and disgrace. Jerusalem’s walls have been pulled down, and its gates have been set ablaze with fire.”
When I heard these words, I sat down and wept, and mourned for days. I was fasting and praying before the God of heaven,
While these things were taking place, the people of Tarsus and Mallus happened to revolt because they had been given as a gift to Antiochis, the king’s concubine.
The king therefore went quickly to settle the matter, leaving Andronicus, one of the men of high rank, as his deputy.
Menelaus, thinking he had found a favourable opportunity, stole some of the temple’s gold objects and gave them to Andronicus. He had also sold others in Tyre and the surrounding cities.
Onias, who had learned these things clearly, denounced them, having withdrawn to a place of asylum at Daphne near Antioch.

Therefore Menelaus took Andronicus aside and urged him to do away with Onias. Andronicus came to Onias, having been persuaded to act deceitfully, greeted him and gave his right hand with oaths. Although under suspicion, he persuaded Onias to leave the asylum and immediately killed him, showing no regard for justice.
For this reason not only Jews but also many of the other nations were indignant and distressed at the man’s unjust murder.
When the king returned from the regions of Cilicia, the Jews in the city petitioned him about the senseless killing of Onias; the Greeks shared their hatred of the wickedness.

Burning with anger, he immediately stripped Andronicus of his purple robe, tore off his tunics, and led him around the whole city to the very place where he had committed the impious act against Onias. There he removed the murderer from life, the Lord rendering him his deserved punishment.
Joab returned from David and sent messengers after Abner. They brought him back from the well of Seiram, but David did not know.
Abner returned to Hebron. Joab took him aside beside the gate to speak with him while lying in wait, and struck him there in the loins. He died for the blood of Asahel, Joab’s brother.
Afterward David heard and said, “I and my kingdom are for ever guiltless before the Lord of the blood of Abner son of Ner.

Let it fall upon Joab’s head and upon his father’s whole house. May Joab’s house never lack someone with a seminal discharge, someone who is leprous, someone holding a staff, someone falling by the sword, or someone lacking bread.”
Joab and Abishai his brother kept watch for Abner because he had put their brother Asahel to death in the battle at Gibeon.

All the people came to have David eat a funeral meal with bread while it was still day. David swore, “May God do these things to me, and add these things: unless the sun sets, I will certainly not taste bread or anything at all.”
All the people understood, and everything the king did before the people pleased them.
All the people and all Israel knew that day that putting Abner son of Ner to death had not come from the king.
The king said to his servants, “Do you not know that a great leader has fallen this day in Israel,
About this time Antiochus organized his second expedition into Egypt.
Throughout the whole city, for nearly forty days, horsemen were seen racing through the air, wearing robes interwoven with gold, armed with lances and arrayed in squadrons; there were drawn swords,
formations of cavalry, attacks and countercharges on either side, movements of shields, masses of spears, volleys of missiles, flashes of golden ornaments, and armour of every kind.
Therefore everyone prayed that the manifestation had come for good.

When a false rumor arose that Antiochus had departed this life, Jason took no fewer than a thousand men and suddenly attacked the city. Those on the wall were driven back, and when the city was finally being taken, Menelaus fled to the citadel.

Jason slaughtered his own fellow citizens without mercy, not realizing that success against his kinsmen was the greatest misfortune. He imagined he was setting up trophies over enemies rather than his own countrymen.
